name: Balkans
summary: The Balkans are a geographical grouping of different states and political traditions. Their kingdoms, empires and principalities do not share a single succession of rulers.

people.resumen: After the Hungarian defeat of Mohi in front of the Mongols, he promoted the reconstruction of the kingdom and the building of stone fortresses. He is reminded of this work as a second founder of Hungary.
He was the last king of Hungary of the Arpád dynasty by male line. His death opened a long competition for the crown in which the Anjou ended up imposing themselves.
Before he succeeded Bela IV, he contested a part of the Hungarian government with his father. His brief independent reign left Ladislao IV, still under the age of six, as his heir.
Carlos Roberto de Anjou affirmed his authority in front of the great Hungarian magnates. The reorganisation of the regent revenues and mining has strengthened the monarchy.
Its proximity to the coumanos caused tensions with the Church and with part of the Hungarian nobility. His reign was marked by internal conflicts and ended with his murder.
The violent death of Wenceslao III extinguished the male line of the Přemysl that ruled Bohemia. His claims about Poland and Hungary show the scope and fragility of that dynastic expansion.
The Polish crown's heritage added a personal union to its Hungarian monarchy. The succession of his daughters Mary and Eduvides then separated the paths of both kingdoms.
He gathered the crowns of Poland and Hungary in full Ottoman expansion. He died in the battle of Varna, whose outcome ended the cross-campaign he was leading.
His access to the Hungarian throne triggered a crisis in which his mother, the magnatos and Carlos de Durazzo competed. His marriage to Seisworld of Luxembourg linked him to the crown.
King of Hungary and Bohemia and later emperor. He participated in the policy of the Great Cysma, the Husito Wars and the Council of Constance, becoming a central figure of the 15th century Europe.

Daughter of Stephen II Kotromanić, she married Louis I of Hungary. Their daughters Mary and Jadwiga continued the family’s connections with the Hungarian and Polish crowns. Her Bosnian origins reveal a family line distinct from that of her cousin Tvrtko, who remained ruler of Bosnia.

people.nombre: Ferdinand I of the Holy Roman Empire
people.resumen: Brother of Charles V and founder of the Austrian branch of the Habsburg. He brought together Austria, Bohemia and a large part of Hungary and finally succeeded his brother in imperial dignity.
He strengthened the Hungarian army and administration and contested territory with the Habsburgs and Jagiellons. His library and court made Buda a centre of Renaissance humanism.
He joined the crowns of Bohemia and Hungary under the Jagellon house. The growing nobility influence limited their ability to act in both kingdoms.
He gathered rights over Austria, Hungary and Bohemia after the death of Seisworld. He was elected King of the Romans, but died without receiving the imperial coronation.
He was born after the death of his father, Albert II, and inherited rights in several Central European territories. His minority turned the effective exercise of power into a dispute.
Emperor Habsburg of relatively conciliating profile in a Europe divided by the Reformation. He also ruled Bohemia and Hungary within the complex Central European monarchy of his house.
Emperor Habsburg who progressively took power from his brother Rodolfo II. His reign prepared the succession and religious crisis that would lead to the Thirty Years' War.

people.nombre: Rudolf II of the Holy Roman Empire
people.resumen: Emperor Habsburg who moved his court to Prague and brought together artists, astronomers and scholars. Their political and religious difficulties weakened their authority in front of other members of the dynasty.

people.nombre: Ferdinand II of the Holy Roman Empire
people.resumen: Emperor Habsburg and fervent advocate of Catholicism. The Bohemia rebellion against his authority triggered the Thirty-Year War, which transformed the political map of the Holy Empire.
King of Hungary since 1172, educhyd in the Byzantine court of Manuel I. His reign strengthened the real administration and expanded Hungarian influence in Dalmatia and Croatia.
King of Hungary since 1196, son of Bela III. His reign was marked by the rebellions of his brother Andrew; he died in 1204 leaving his son Ladislaus III.
Son of Emerico, crowned king of Hungary as a child in 1204. His uncle Andrés took over the government; the little king died in Austrian exile in 1205.
The Golden Bullet limited certain regious prerogatives and recognized rights to the Hungarian nobles. He also directed a cross-expedition to the Holy Land.
He died in the defeat of Mohács in front of Soliman the Magnificent. His death opened the competition between Fernando de Habsburg and Juan de Zápolya for the Hungarian crown.

people.nombre: Charles III of Naples and II of Hungary
people.resumen: Charles of Durazzo governed Croatia and Dalmatia on behalf of Louis I before conquering Naples in 1381. His lands included Corfu and Butrint, while his authority over Achaea was nominal in the face of the local power of the Navarrese Company. Crowned king of Hungary and Croatia on 31 December 1385, he was attacked at Buda in February 1386 and died soon afterwards. His title to Jerusalem did not imply control of the Holy Land.

people.nombre: Ferdinand III of the Holy Roman Empire
people.resumen: Emperor during the final phase of the Thirty Years' War. He participated in the negotiation of the political order that culminated in the Peace of Westphalia in 1648.

people.nombre: Leopold I of the Holy Roman Empire
people.resumen: Emperor Habsburg for almost half a century. His reign was marked by the wars against Louis XIV and the great confrontation with the Ottoman Empire, which ended in Vienna in 1683.

people.nombre: Joseph I of the Holy Roman Empire
people.resumen: Emperor Habsburg during the Spanish War of Succession. He continued his father's policy, Leopold I, and supported his brother Carlos's candidacy for the Spanish throne.

people.nombre: Charles VI of the Holy Roman Empire
people.resumen: Emperor Habsburg and rival of Philip V in the War of Succession. His house ruled Milan, Naples and Sardinia on different dates; he exchanged Sardinia for Sicily in 1720. The Pragmatic Healing sought to secure her inheritance to Mary Teresa.

Sovereign of the hereditary domains of the Habsburgans and one of the great figures of the 18th century. He defended his inheritance in the Austrian War of Succession and promoted important administrative reforms.

people.nombre: Joseph II of the Holy Roman Empire
people.resumen: Emperor Habsburg associated with the illustrated despotism. It tried to profoundly modernize the administration, the Church and society of its territories through a very ambitious reform programme.

people.nombre: Leopold II of the Holy Roman Empire
people.resumen: Emperor Habsburg of brief reign, which was succeeded after ruling Tuscany. It moderated several reforms of Joseph II and faced the expansion of the French Revolution in Europe.

people.nombre: Francis II of the Holy Roman Empire
people.resumen: The last emperor of the Holy Empire and first emperor of Austria since 1804. He fought revolutionary and Napoleonic France, dissolved the Empire in 1806 and married his daughter Maria Luisa to Napoleon.
Daughter of Serbian lord Constantine Dragaš and wife of Manuel II Paleologist. She was the mother of the last two Byzantine emperors, John VIII and Constantine XI.
Tsar of Bulgaria, 1186–1196. Tsar of the Asen dynasty.
Consort of the Asen dynasty. Their career was connected to Bulgaria.

Tsar of Bulgaria that consolidated the restoration of the Bulgarian state against Byzantium and fought the newly created Latin Empire. His victory over the Crusaders in Adrianópolis turned Bulgaria into a first-class Balkan power.
Tsar of Bulgaria, 1207–1218. Tsar of the House of Asen.
The Bulgarian Tsar under whose reign the Second Bulgarian Empire reached one of its most powerful moments. Klokotnitsa's victory in 1230 extended its influence to a large part of the Balkans.
Consort of the Árpád dynasty. Their career was connected to Hungary, Bulgaria.
Consort of the Ducas dynasty. Their career was connected to Epirus, Bulgaria.
Consort of the Asen dynasty. Their career was connected to Bulgaria, Serbia.

Tar of Bulgaria for much of the 14th century. His long reign coincided with a remarkable cultural flowering, but also with the political fragmentation that preceded the Ottoman advance.
Consort of the Basarab dynasty. Their career was connected to Wallachia, Bulgaria.
Consort, their career was connected to Bulgaria.
Tsar of Bulgaria, 1360–1396 (Branch rule). Tsar of the Shishman dynasty.
One of the last zars of the Second Bulgarian Empire. Tarnovo ruled during the Ottoman advance and his defeat symbolizes the end of independent medieval Bulgaria.
A sister of the Bulgarian tsar Ivan Alexander and wife of Stefan Dušan of Serbia, she served as regent for their son Stefan Uroš V and ended her life as a nun.
Consort of the Shishman dynasty. Their life was connected with Bulgaria and Bosnia.
Great župan of Serbia, 1166–1196. Great župan of the Nemanjić dynasty.
Consort, their career was connected to Serbia.
First crowned king of the Nemanjić dynasty. His reign consolidated Serbia's political independence and opened the monarchical stage that would culminate in the empire of Stefan Dušan.
Consort of the House of Dandolo. Their life was connected with Venice, Serbia.
The son of Stephen the First Coronado, king of Serbia between 1228 and 1233. His brother, Esteban Vladislav, put him from his throne.
King of Serbia between 1234 and 1243 after displacing his brother Radoslav. He was in turn replaced by his younger brother, Stephen Uroš I.
He developed mining and trade with Ragusa, was deposed by his son Dragutin and ended his life as a monk.
Consort. Their career was connected to France, Serbia.
King of Serbia from 1276 after deposing his father Stefan Uroš I. He ceded the throne to his brother Milutin in 1282 and thereafter ruled a separate northern realm around Belgrade and Syrmia.
Consort of the House of Árpád. Their life was connected with Hungary, Serbia.
King Nemanjić who expanded Serbia to Macedonia and strengthened its ties with Byzantium. His reign was decisive for the territorial and cultural growth of the Serbian kingdom.
King of Serbia since 1321, son of Milutin. He beat the Bulgarians in Velbazhd (1330), founded the monastery of Visoki Dečani and was deposed by his son Esteban Dušan.
Consort of the Smilets dynasty. Their career was connected to Bulgaria and Serbia.

King of Serbia and, since 1346, emperor of Serbs and Greeks. He built the largest medieval Serbian state and promulgated an important legal code, although his empire was fragmented shortly after his death.
Son of Esteban Dušan and last emperor of the Nemanjić dynasty. During his reign the great lords became independent and the Serbian Empire was fragmented.

Serbian prince who emerged as one of the main authorities after the disintegration of the Dušan empire. He died at the Battle of Kosovo in 1389, then turned into a central episode of Serbian historical memory.
Regent of Serbia, 1389–1393. Princess of the Nemanjić dynasty.
The son of Lazar Hrebeljanoć and his desspot from Serbia. He sailed between the Ottoman pressure and the Hungarian influence while turning Belgrade into an important political and cultural centre.
Noble of the Lazarević dynasty. Their career was connected to Serbia.
Lord of Kosovo, 1373–1396. Lord of the House of Branković.
He succeeded his uncle Stefan Lazarević and organized his power center in Smederevo. The Ottoman conquest interrupted his government between 1439 and 1444.
Consort of the Kantakouzenos dynasty. Their career was connected to Byzantium and Serbia.
Despot of Serbia, 1458–1459. Despot of the Branković dynasty.
Despot of Serbia, 1456–1458. Despot of the House of Branković.
Consort of the House of Branković. Their life was connected with Serbia, Bosnia.
Founder of Wallachia’s first stable ruling dynasty. His victory over Charles I of Hungary at Posada in 1330 secured broad autonomy for the principality north of the Danube.
Voivode of Wallachia, 1352–1364. Voivode of the House of Basarab.
Voivode of Wallachia, 1364–1377. Voivode of the Basarab dynasty.
Voivode of Wallachia, 1377–1383. Voivode of the Basarab dynasty.
Consort. Their life was connected with Wallachia.
Voivode of Wallachia, 1383–1386. Voivode of the Basarab dynasty.
Voivode of Wallachia during a phase of expansion and consolidation. He resisted Ottoman pressure and made the Danube frontier one of the principal political theatres of south-eastern Europe.

Voivode of Wallachia and a member of the Order of the Dragon, from which the name Dracul derives. His policies were shaped by the rivalry between Hungary and the Ottoman Empire and by Wallachia’s unstable succession.

Voivode de Wallachia known as Vlad-epeș, "the Empalator."His violent struggle for power and his confrontation with Mehmed II nurtured a reputation that centuries later would be transformed by literature into the myth of Dracula.

Brother of Vlad III and rival for the throne of Wallachia. With Ottoman support he replaced Vlad during the 1462 crisis and embodies the complex policy of accommodation and resistance to Constantinople.
Voivode of Moldova, 1359–1367. Prince of the Bogdan-Mușat dynasty.
Voivode of Moldova, 1368–1375. Prince of the Bogdan-Mușat dynasty.

Voivode of Moldavia, 1375–1391. Prince of the Bogdan-Mușat dynasty.
Voivode of Moldavia, 1391–1394. Prince of the House of Bogdana-Mușat.
Prince of Moldova, remembered for a long period of political stability. He strengthened the institutions of the principality and maneuvered between Poland, Hungary and its Black Sea neighbours.
Voivode of Moldova, 1449–1451. Prince of the Bogdan-Mușat dynasty.
A noblewoman whose career was connected with Moldavia.

Prince of Moldavia for almost half a century and one of the central figures of fifteenth-century eastern Europe. He defended his principality against the Ottomans, Poles and Hungarians and became associated with an energetic military and religious policy.
Consort of the Basarab dynasty. Their career was connected to Wallachia, Moldova.
Voivode of Moldavia, 1504–1517. Prince of the Bogdan-Mușat dynasty.

Prince of Moldova and son of Stephen the Great. He tried to maintain an active policy between Poland, Hungary and the Ottoman Empire during a time when Moldovan autonomy was increasingly difficult to sustain.

He consolidated his government after the fall of power of Mladen II Šubić. The expansion to Hum and the commercial relations with Dubrovnik reinforced the Bosnian position in the Adriatic. His daughter Elizabeth married Louis I of Hungary; the banate passed to his nephew Tvrtko, son of Vladislav.

Brother of Stephen II and husband of Jelena Šubić, links the leading families of Bosnia and Croatia. His son Tvrtko inherited the banate as a young man. The participation of their parents in that first stage helps to understand that ownership and exercise of power were not always the same.

Member of the Šubić of Bribir, married Vladislav of Bosnia and was mother of Tvrtko I. His intervention during the youth of the future king places this Croatian noble at the centre of Bosnian continuity. The family connection did not make the Kotromanić a male branch of the Šubić.
He inherited the banate of his uncle Esteban II. After being displaced by his brother in 1366, he regained power the following year.
King of Bosnia, 1391–1395. King of the Kotromanić dynasty.

Widow of Dabiša, was recognized as queen by Bosnian magnates in 1395. Their access is not explained by a filiation between two consecutive sovereign, but by a political decision of the nobility. She lost the throne in 1398 and still is alive in 1399.
King of Bosnia between 1398 and 1404 and again between 1409 and 1418, sustained or deposed according to the alliances of the great Bosnian magnates and the pressure of Hungary.
King of Bosnia in 1404–1409 and again from 1421 to 1443. He sought Hungarian support against growing Ottoman pressure and the rivalry of the magnates.
King of Bosnia in the decades before the Ottoman conquest. His reign was marked by internal religious tensions and the growing pressure of Hungary and Mehmed II.
A daughter of Stephen Vukčić Kosača, she married Stephen Thomas of Bosnia in 1446. The marriage brought the monarchy closer to one of the region’s greatest powers.
Son of Stephen Thomas and Vojača, he married Jelena, daughter of the Serbian despot Lazar Branković. The link accompanied its short Serbian access of 1459, before the fall of Smedereo.

He allied with the Habsburg with the Ottoman and defeated Andres Bathory in 1599. He ruled Valacia, Transylvania and Moldova for a few months with different roles and legititivities. The personal union was brief and did not create a modern national state.
Ban of Croatia from 1542 to 1556, he combined military service to the Habsburgs with the consolidation of his family estates. He died defending Szigetvár against Suleiman.
people.biografia: Ban of Croatia from 1542 to 1556, he combined military service to the Habsburgs with the consolidation of his family estates. He died defending Szigetvár against Suleiman. His marriage to Katarina Frankopan and the descendants of his son Juraj trace the links that eventually connected the Zrinskis with Transylvania.

people.resumen: First wife of Nikola IV Zrinski and mother of Juraj IV, connects two of the great Croatian houses. She died before the Szigetvár defender. She should be distinguished from Anne Katarina Frankopan, a writer from the next century and wife of Petar Zrinski.

The son of Nikola IV and Katarina Frankopan, developed their activity between the Croatian and Hungarian domains of the family. He exercised military command and favored the printing. He was the father of Juraj V; his importance in the continuity of the lineage should not be confused with the exercise of the position of ban.

Ban of Croatia between 1622 and 1626, was the son of Juraj IV and father of Nikola VII and Petar IV. His conversion to Catholicism marked the religious politics of his domains. The short duration of his government contrasts with the later projection of his two sons.
The military and poet celebrated the defense of Szigetvár by his great-grandfather. He was appointed to ban in 1647 and took an oath to the king the following year.

A brother of Nikola VII, he was appointed ban in 1665, although his formal installation was delayed until 1668. Alongside his brother-in-law Fran Krsto Frankopan, he took part in noble opposition to the Habsburgs.
people.biografia: A brother of Nikola VII, he was appointed ban in 1665, although his formal installation was delayed until 1668. Alongside his brother-in-law Fran Krsto Frankopan, he took part in noble opposition to the Habsburgs. He lost office in 1670 and was executed in 1671. His daughter Jelena continued the family connection with the Rákóczis.

people.resumen: The military of the Frankopan house, acted on the Croatian border and on the coast. He was the father of Ana Katarina and Fran Krsto, born of different marriages. Incorporating it allows us to recognize the relationship between two protagonists of the culture and the political conflicts of Croatia of the 17th century.
A writer and administrator of her family’s estates, she married Petar Zrinski. She took part in her circle’s diplomatic efforts and published a devotional work in Venice.
Poet and noble Croatian, he was half-brother of Anne Katarina Frankopan. His Italian ties and marriage extended his political horizon.
The daughter of Petar Zrinski and Anne Katarina Frankopan, she married Francis I Rákóczi and was the mother of Francis II. She defended Munkács against the imperial forces.

Ban documented since 1290, ruled at a time of increasing intervention by the Šubićs in Bosnia. He disappeared from the news after the confrontation of 1302. His sons Stephen II and Vladislav lead to two roads of the house: Queen Elizabeth of Hungary and King Tvrtko I.

Wife of Stephen I Kotroman and mother of Esteban II and Vladislav, is part of the Serbian descent invoked by the Kotromanić. Her grandchildren Isabel of Bosnia and Tvrtko I allow to follow different connections: the Hungarian monarchy and the construction of Bosnian royalty.
He succeeded his uncle Sandalj in a powerful regional heritage. Since 1448 he has used the ducal title associated with San Sava, from which the name Herzegovina comes.

Wife of Stefan Branković, shared the family's displacement after the loss of Serbian power. Her sons Đorđe and Jovan preserved the dignity of despots in the Hungarian sphere. Her religious memory was linked to Krušedol and the preservation of the dynastic tradition in exile.

The son of Stefan and Angelina, he retained the title of Serbian despot in exile. He left the secular life and took the name of Maximus. His religious activity and his relationship with Krušedol continued the presence of the family in the region. It should not be confused with the 17th century homonymous historian.

The son of Stefan and Angelina, he initially shared the dignity of despot with his brother Đorđe. The title was held in the Hungarian political sphere and did not entail the recovery of Serbia. His daughter Elena married Petru Rareș, so the descendants of the Branković linked with the Moldovan court.

A daughter of Jovan Branković and wife of Petru Rareș, she brought a connection with the Serbian despots to Moldavia. She took part in government during her son Stephen’s minority. Her daughter Ruxandra also became a Moldavian consort and regent; Chiajna, Petru’s daughter by another union, was her stepdaughter.

The son of Vlad II Dracul, briefly came to power in 1481 and recovered him the following year. His continuity until 1495 opens a family path different from that of his brother Vlad III. His son Radu the Great extended this Basarab line in the Wallachia government.

He succeeded his father Vlad Călugărul. His government combined relations with the neighbouring powers and religious patronage, including the Dealu monastery. The offspring of his son Mircea Ciobanul connected this Walloon line with the Rareș of Moldova, without bringing together both principalities.
A son of Radu the Great, he ruled Wallachia in three separate periods interrupted by depositions and restorations. He married Chiajna, daughter of Petru Rareș of Moldavia.

Daughter of Petru Rareș and her first wife Maria, she married Mircea Ciobanul. After her husband’s death she directed the government of her son Petru. Her deposition in 1568 drove the family into exile. She is still recorded in 1587, but the precise year of her death is unknown.
The son of Mircea Ciobanul and Chiajna, he accepted the principality at the age of twelve. His mother maintained a decisive intervention in the government.

The daughter of Petru Rareș and Elena Branković, she married Alejandro Lăpușneanu. She intervened in the continuity of her family and, after the removal and death of her husband, exercised the regency of Bogdan IV. Her ancestry links the Moldovan sovereigns with the family of the Serbian despots.
He ruled Moldova in two stages, separated by a deposition. His marriage to Ruxandra Rareș strengthened the links with the offspring of Petru Rareș.
A son of Alexandru Lăpușneanu and Ruxandra Rareș, he acceded during his minority, with his mother serving as regent until 1570.
people.biografia: A son of Alexandru Lăpușneanu and Ruxandra Rareș, he acceded during his minority, with his mother serving as regent until 1570. Relations with Poland and internal conflicts shaped his position towards the Ottomans. He lost power in 1572; kinship had not guaranteed a stable succession.

Sovereign of the hereditary domains of the Habsburgans and one of the great figures of the 18th century. He defended his inheritance in the Austrian War of Succession and promoted important administrative reforms.

persona.nombre: Joseph II of the Holy Roman Empire
persona.resumen: Emperor Habsburg associated with the illustrated despotism. It tried to profoundly modernize the administration, the Church and society of its territories through a very ambitious reform programme.

persona.nombre: Leopold II of the Holy Roman Empire
persona.resumen: Emperor Habsburg of brief reign, which was succeeded after ruling Tuscany. It moderated several reforms of Joseph II and faced the expansion of the French Revolution in Europe.

persona.resumen: The last emperor of the Holy Empire and first emperor of Austria since 1804. He fought revolutionary and Napoleonic France, dissolved the Empire in 1806 and married his daughter Maria Luisa to Napoleon.

personas.resumen: After the Hungarian defeat of Mohi in front of the Mongols, he promoted the reconstruction of the kingdom and the building of stone fortresses. He is reminded of this work as a second founder of Hungary.
He was the last king of Hungary of the Arpád dynasty by male line. His death opened a long competition for the crown in which the Anjou ended up imposing themselves.
Before he succeeded Bela IV, he contested a part of the Hungarian government with his father. His brief independent reign left Ladislao IV, still under the age of six, as his heir.
Carlos Roberto de Anjou affirmed his authority in front of the great Hungarian magnates. The reorganisation of the regent revenues and mining has strengthened the monarchy.
Its proximity to the coumanos caused tensions with the Church and with part of the Hungarian nobility. His reign was marked by internal conflicts and ended with his murder.
The violent death of Wenceslao III extinguished the male line of the Přemysl that ruled Bohemia. His claims about Poland and Hungary show the scope and fragility of that dynastic expansion.
The Polish crown's heritage added a personal union to its Hungarian monarchy. The succession of his daughters Mary and Eduvides then separated the paths of both kingdoms.
He gathered the crowns of Poland and Hungary in full Ottoman expansion. He died in the battle of Varna, whose outcome ended the cross-campaign he was leading.
His access to the Hungarian throne triggered a crisis in which his mother, the magnatos and Carlos de Durazzo competed. His marriage to Seisworld of Luxembourg linked him to the crown.
King of Hungary and Bohemia and later emperor. He participated in the policy of the Great Cysma, the Husito Wars and the Council of Constance, becoming a central figure of the 15th century Europe.

Daughter of Stephen II Kotromanić, she married Louis I of Hungary. Their daughters Mary and Jadwiga continued the family’s connections with the Hungarian and Polish crowns. Her Bosnian origins reveal a family line distinct from that of her cousin Tvrtko, who remained ruler of Bosnia.

personas.nombre: Ferdinand I of the Holy Roman Empire
personas.resumen: Brother of Charles V and founder of the Austrian branch of the Habsburg. He brought together Austria, Bohemia and a large part of Hungary and finally succeeded his brother in imperial dignity.
He strengthened the Hungarian army and administration and contested territory with the Habsburgs and Jagiellons. His library and court made Buda a centre of Renaissance humanism.
He joined the crowns of Bohemia and Hungary under the Jagellon house. The growing nobility influence limited their ability to act in both kingdoms.
He gathered rights over Austria, Hungary and Bohemia after the death of Seisworld. He was elected King of the Romans, but died without receiving the imperial coronation.
He was born after the death of his father, Albert II, and inherited rights in several Central European territories. His minority turned the effective exercise of power into a dispute.
Emperor Habsburg of relatively conciliating profile in a Europe divided by the Reformation. He also ruled Bohemia and Hungary within the complex Central European monarchy of his house.
Emperor Habsburg who progressively took power from his brother Rodolfo II. His reign prepared the succession and religious crisis that would lead to the Thirty Years' War.

personas.nombre: Rudolf II of the Holy Roman Empire
personas.resumen: Emperor Habsburg who moved his court to Prague and brought together artists, astronomers and scholars. Their political and religious difficulties weakened their authority in front of other members of the dynasty.

personas.nombre: Ferdinand II of the Holy Roman Empire
personas.resumen: Emperor Habsburg and fervent advocate of Catholicism. The Bohemia rebellion against his authority triggered the Thirty-Year War, which transformed the political map of the Holy Empire.
King of Hungary since 1172, educhyd in the Byzantine court of Manuel I. His reign strengthened the real administration and expanded Hungarian influence in Dalmatia and Croatia.
King of Hungary since 1196, son of Bela III. His reign was marked by the rebellions of his brother Andrew; he died in 1204 leaving his son Ladislaus III.
Son of Emerico, crowned king of Hungary as a child in 1204. His uncle Andrés took over the government; the little king died in Austrian exile in 1205.
The Golden Bullet limited certain regious prerogatives and recognized rights to the Hungarian nobles. He also directed a cross-expedition to the Holy Land.
He died in the defeat of Mohács in front of Soliman the Magnificent. His death opened the competition between Fernando de Habsburg and Juan de Zápolya for the Hungarian crown.

personas.nombre: Charles III of Naples and II of Hungary
personas.resumen: Charles of Durazzo governed Croatia and Dalmatia on behalf of Louis I before conquering Naples in 1381. His lands included Corfu and Butrint, while his authority over Achaea was nominal in the face of the local power of the Navarrese Company. Crowned king of Hungary and Croatia on 31 December 1385, he was attacked at Buda in February 1386 and died soon afterwards. His title to Jerusalem did not imply control of the Holy Land.

Daughter of Serbian lord Constantine Dragaš and wife of Manuel II Paleologist. She was the mother of the last two Byzantine emperors, John VIII and Constantine XI.
Tsar of Bulgaria, 1186–1196. Tsar of the Asen dynasty.
Consort of the Asen dynasty. Their career was connected to Bulgaria.

Tsar of Bulgaria that consolidated the restoration of the Bulgarian state against Byzantium and fought the newly created Latin Empire. His victory over the Crusaders in Adrianópolis turned Bulgaria into a first-class Balkan power.
Tsar of Bulgaria, 1207–1218. Tsar of the House of Asen.
The Bulgarian Tsar under whose reign the Second Bulgarian Empire reached one of its most powerful moments. Klokotnitsa's victory in 1230 extended its influence to a large part of the Balkans.
Consort of the Árpád dynasty. Their career was connected to Hungary, Bulgaria.
Consort of the Ducas dynasty. Their career was connected to Epirus, Bulgaria.
Consort of the Asen dynasty. Their career was connected to Bulgaria, Serbia.
Tsar of Bulgaria, 1241–1246. Tsar of the Asen dynasty.
Tsar of Bulgaria, 1246–1256. Tsar of the House of Asen.

Despot of the House of Shishman. Their life was connected with Bulgaria.
A noble of House Shishman whose life was connected with Bulgaria.
Tar of Bulgaria for much of the 14th century. His long reign coincided with a remarkable cultural flowering, but also with the political fragmentation that preceded the Ottoman advance.
Consort of the Basarab dynasty. Their career was connected to Wallachia, Bulgaria.
Consort, their career was connected to Bulgaria.
Tsar of Bulgaria, 1360–1396 (Branch rule). Tsar of the Shishman dynasty.
One of the last zars of the Second Bulgarian Empire. Tarnovo ruled during the Ottoman advance and his defeat symbolizes the end of independent medieval Bulgaria.
A sister of the Bulgarian tsar Ivan Alexander and wife of Stefan Dušan of Serbia, she served as regent for their son Stefan Uroš V and ended her life as a nun.
Consort of the Shishman dynasty. Their life was connected with Bulgaria and Bosnia.
Great župan of Serbia, 1166–1196. Great župan of the Nemanjić dynasty.
Consort, their career was connected to Serbia.
First crowned king of the Nemanjić dynasty. His reign consolidated Serbia's political independence and opened the monarchical stage that would culminate in the empire of Stefan Dušan.
Consort of the House of Dandolo. Their life was connected with Venice, Serbia.
The son of Stephen the First Coronado, king of Serbia between 1228 and 1233. His brother, Esteban Vladislav, put him from his throne.
King of Serbia between 1234 and 1243 after displacing his brother Radoslav. He was in turn replaced by his younger brother, Stephen Uroš I.
He developed mining and trade with Ragusa, was deposed by his son Dragutin and ended his life as a monk.
Consort. Their career was connected to France, Serbia.
King of Serbia from 1276 after deposing his father Stefan Uroš I. He ceded the throne to his brother Milutin in 1282 and thereafter ruled a separate northern realm around Belgrade and Syrmia.
Consort of the House of Árpád. Their life was connected with Hungary, Serbia.
King Nemanjić who expanded Serbia to Macedonia and strengthened its ties with Byzantium. His reign was decisive for the territorial and cultural growth of the Serbian kingdom.
King of Serbia since 1321, son of Milutin. He beat the Bulgarians in Velbazhd (1330), founded the monastery of Visoki Dečani and was deposed by his son Esteban Dušan.
Consort of the Smilets dynasty. Their career was connected to Bulgaria and Serbia.

King of Serbia and, since 1346, emperor of Serbs and Greeks. He built the largest medieval Serbian state and promulgated an important legal code, although his empire was fragmented shortly after his death.
Son of Esteban Dušan and last emperor of the Nemanjić dynasty. During his reign the great lords became independent and the Serbian Empire was fragmented.

Serbian prince who emerged as one of the main authorities after the disintegration of the Dušan empire. He died at the Battle of Kosovo in 1389, then turned into a central episode of Serbian historical memory.
Regent of Serbia, 1389–1393. Princess of the Nemanjić dynasty.
The son of Lazar Hrebeljanoć and his desspot from Serbia. He sailed between the Ottoman pressure and the Hungarian influence while turning Belgrade into an important political and cultural centre.
Noble of the Lazarević dynasty. Their career was connected to Serbia.
Lord of Kosovo, 1373–1396. Lord of the House of Branković.
He succeeded his uncle Stefan Lazarević and organized his power center in Smederevo. The Ottoman conquest interrupted his government between 1439 and 1444.
Consort of the Kantakouzenos dynasty. Their career was connected to Byzantium and Serbia.
Despot of Serbia, 1458–1459. Despot of the Branković dynasty.
Despot of Serbia, 1456–1458. Despot of the House of Branković.
Consort of the House of Branković. Their life was connected with Serbia, Bosnia.
Founder of Wallachia’s first stable ruling dynasty. His victory over Charles I of Hungary at Posada in 1330 secured broad autonomy for the principality north of the Danube.
Voivode of Wallachia, 1352–1364. Voivode of the House of Basarab.
Voivode of Wallachia, 1364–1377. Voivode of the Basarab dynasty.
Voivode of Wallachia, 1377–1383. Voivode of the Basarab dynasty.
Consort. Their life was connected with Wallachia.
Voivode of Wallachia, 1383–1386. Voivode of the Basarab dynasty.
Voivode of Wallachia during a phase of expansion and consolidation. He resisted Ottoman pressure and made the Danube frontier one of the principal political theatres of south-eastern Europe.

Voivode of Wallachia and a member of the Order of the Dragon, from which the name Dracul derives. His policies were shaped by the rivalry between Hungary and the Ottoman Empire and by Wallachia’s unstable succession.

Voivode de Wallachia known as Vlad-epeș, "the Empalator."His violent struggle for power and his confrontation with Mehmed II nurtured a reputation that centuries later would be transformed by literature into the myth of Dracula.

Brother of Vlad III and rival for the throne of Wallachia. With Ottoman support he replaced Vlad during the 1462 crisis and embodies the complex policy of accommodation and resistance to Constantinople.
Voivode of Moldova, 1359–1367. Prince of the Bogdan-Mușat dynasty.
Voivode of Moldova, 1368–1375. Prince of the Bogdan-Mușat dynasty.
A noble of House Bogdan-Mușat whose life was connected with Moldova.
Noble of the Bogdan-Mușat dynasty. Their career was connected to Moldova.
Voivode of Moldavia, 1375–1391. Prince of the Bogdan-Mușat dynasty.
Voivode of Moldavia, 1391–1394. Prince of the House of Bogdana-Mușat.
Prince of Moldova, remembered for a long period of political stability. He strengthened the institutions of the principality and maneuvered between Poland, Hungary and its Black Sea neighbours.
Voivode of Moldova, 1449–1451. Prince of the Bogdan-Mușat dynasty.
A noblewoman whose career was connected with Moldavia.

Prince of Moldavia for almost half a century and one of the central figures of fifteenth-century eastern Europe. He defended his principality against the Ottomans, Poles and Hungarians and became associated with an energetic military and religious policy.
Consort of the Basarab dynasty. Their career was connected to Wallachia, Moldova.
Voivode of Moldavia, 1504–1517. Prince of the Bogdan-Mușat dynasty.

Prince of Moldova and son of Stephen the Great. He tried to maintain an active policy between Poland, Hungary and the Ottoman Empire during a time when Moldovan autonomy was increasingly difficult to sustain.

He consolidated his government after the fall of power of Mladen II Šubić. The expansion to Hum and the commercial relations with Dubrovnik reinforced the Bosnian position in the Adriatic. His daughter Elizabeth married Louis I of Hungary; the banate passed to his nephew Tvrtko, son of Vladislav.

Brother of Stephen II and husband of Jelena Šubić, links the leading families of Bosnia and Croatia. His son Tvrtko inherited the banate as a young man. The participation of their parents in that first stage helps to understand that ownership and exercise of power were not always the same.

Member of the Šubić of Bribir, married Vladislav of Bosnia and was mother of Tvrtko I. His intervention during the youth of the future king places this Croatian noble at the centre of Bosnian continuity. The family connection did not make the Kotromanić a male branch of the Šubić.
He inherited the banate of his uncle Esteban II. After being displaced by his brother in 1366, he regained power the following year.
King of Bosnia, 1391–1395. King of the Kotromanić dynasty.

Widow of Dabiša, was recognized as queen by Bosnian magnates in 1395. Their access is not explained by a filiation between two consecutive sovereign, but by a political decision of the nobility. She lost the throne in 1398 and still is alive in 1399.
King of Bosnia between 1398 and 1404 and again between 1409 and 1418, sustained or deposed according to the alliances of the great Bosnian magnates and the pressure of Hungary.
King of Bosnia in 1404–1409 and again from 1421 to 1443. He sought Hungarian support against growing Ottoman pressure and the rivalry of the magnates.
King of Bosnia in the decades before the Ottoman conquest. His reign was marked by internal religious tensions and the growing pressure of Hungary and Mehmed II.
A daughter of Stephen Vukčić Kosača, she married Stephen Thomas of Bosnia in 1446. The marriage brought the monarchy closer to one of the region’s greatest powers.
Son of Stephen Thomas and Vojača, he married Jelena, daughter of the Serbian despot Lazar Branković. The link accompanied its short Serbian access of 1459, before the fall of Smedereo.

He allied with the Habsburg with the Ottoman and defeated Andres Bathory in 1599. He ruled Valacia, Transylvania and Moldova for a few months with different roles and legititivities. The personal union was brief and did not create a modern national state.
Ban of Croatia from 1542 to 1556, he combined military service to the Habsburgs with the consolidation of his family estates. He died defending Szigetvár against Suleiman.
personas.biografia: Ban of Croatia from 1542 to 1556, he combined military service to the Habsburgs with the consolidation of his family estates. He died defending Szigetvár against Suleiman. His marriage to Katarina Frankopan and the descendants of his son Juraj trace the links that eventually connected the Zrinskis with Transylvania.

personas.resumen: First wife of Nikola IV Zrinski and mother of Juraj IV, connects two of the great Croatian houses. She died before the Szigetvár defender. She should be distinguished from Anne Katarina Frankopan, a writer from the next century and wife of Petar Zrinski.

The son of Nikola IV and Katarina Frankopan, developed their activity between the Croatian and Hungarian domains of the family. He exercised military command and favored the printing. He was the father of Juraj V; his importance in the continuity of the lineage should not be confused with the exercise of the position of ban.

Ban of Croatia between 1622 and 1626, was the son of Juraj IV and father of Nikola VII and Petar IV. His conversion to Catholicism marked the religious politics of his domains. The short duration of his government contrasts with the later projection of his two sons.
The military and poet celebrated the defense of Szigetvár by his great-grandfather. He was appointed to ban in 1647 and took an oath to the king the following year.

A brother of Nikola VII, he was appointed ban in 1665, although his formal installation was delayed until 1668. Alongside his brother-in-law Fran Krsto Frankopan, he took part in noble opposition to the Habsburgs.
personas.biografia: A brother of Nikola VII, he was appointed ban in 1665, although his formal installation was delayed until 1668. Alongside his brother-in-law Fran Krsto Frankopan, he took part in noble opposition to the Habsburgs. He lost office in 1670 and was executed in 1671. His daughter Jelena continued the family connection with the Rákóczis.

personas.resumen: The military of the Frankopan house, acted on the Croatian border and on the coast. He was the father of Ana Katarina and Fran Krsto, born of different marriages. Incorporating it allows us to recognize the relationship between two protagonists of the culture and the political conflicts of Croatia of the 17th century.
A writer and administrator of her family’s estates, she married Petar Zrinski. She took part in her circle’s diplomatic efforts and published a devotional work in Venice.
Poet and noble Croatian, he was half-brother of Anne Katarina Frankopan. His Italian ties and marriage extended his political horizon.
The daughter of Petar Zrinski and Anne Katarina Frankopan, she married Francis I Rákóczi and was the mother of Francis II. She defended Munkács against the imperial forces.

Ban documented since 1290, ruled at a time of increasing intervention by the Šubićs in Bosnia. He disappeared from the news after the confrontation of 1302. His sons Stephen II and Vladislav lead to two roads of the house: Queen Elizabeth of Hungary and King Tvrtko I.

Wife of Stephen I Kotroman and mother of Esteban II and Vladislav, is part of the Serbian descent invoked by the Kotromanić. Her grandchildren Isabel of Bosnia and Tvrtko I allow to follow different connections: the Hungarian monarchy and the construction of Bosnian royalty.
He succeeded his uncle Sandalj in a powerful regional heritage. Since 1448 he has used the ducal title associated with San Sava, from which the name Herzegovina comes.

Wife of Stefan Branković, shared the family's displacement after the loss of Serbian power. Her sons Đorđe and Jovan preserved the dignity of despots in the Hungarian sphere. Her religious memory was linked to Krušedol and the preservation of the dynastic tradition in exile.

The son of Stefan and Angelina, he retained the title of Serbian despot in exile. He left the secular life and took the name of Maximus. His religious activity and his relationship with Krušedol continued the presence of the family in the region. It should not be confused with the 17th century homonymous historian.

The son of Stefan and Angelina, he initially shared the dignity of despot with his brother Đorđe. The title was held in the Hungarian political sphere and did not entail the recovery of Serbia. His daughter Elena married Petru Rareș, so the descendants of the Branković linked with the Moldovan court.

A daughter of Jovan Branković and wife of Petru Rareș, she brought a connection with the Serbian despots to Moldavia. She took part in government during her son Stephen’s minority. Her daughter Ruxandra also became a Moldavian consort and regent; Chiajna, Petru’s daughter by another union, was her stepdaughter.

The son of Vlad II Dracul, briefly came to power in 1481 and recovered him the following year. His continuity until 1495 opens a family path different from that of his brother Vlad III. His son Radu the Great extended this Basarab line in the Wallachia government.

He succeeded his father Vlad Călugărul. His government combined relations with the neighbouring powers and religious patronage, including the Dealu monastery. The offspring of his son Mircea Ciobanul connected this Walloon line with the Rareș of Moldova, without bringing together both principalities.
A son of Radu the Great, he ruled Wallachia in three separate periods interrupted by depositions and restorations. He married Chiajna, daughter of Petru Rareș of Moldavia.

Daughter of Petru Rareș and her first wife Maria, she married Mircea Ciobanul. After her husband’s death she directed the government of her son Petru. Her deposition in 1568 drove the family into exile. She is still recorded in 1587, but the precise year of her death is unknown.
The son of Mircea Ciobanul and Chiajna, he accepted the principality at the age of twelve. His mother maintained a decisive intervention in the government.

The daughter of Petru Rareș and Elena Branković, she married Alejandro Lăpușneanu. She intervened in the continuity of her family and, after the removal and death of her husband, exercised the regency of Bogdan IV. Her ancestry links the Moldovan sovereigns with the family of the Serbian despots.
He ruled Moldova in two stages, separated by a deposition. His marriage to Ruxandra Rareș strengthened the links with the offspring of Petru Rareș.
A son of Alexandru Lăpușneanu and Ruxandra Rareș, he acceded during his minority, with his mother serving as regent until 1570.
personas.biografia: A son of Alexandru Lăpușneanu and Ruxandra Rareș, he acceded during his minority, with his mother serving as regent until 1570. Relations with Poland and internal conflicts shaped his position towards the Ottomans. He lost power in 1572; kinship had not guaranteed a stable succession.

eventos.descripcion: The agreement legally accepts the coexistence of Catholic and Lutheran territories within the Empire and recognizes that religious unity can no longer be restored by mere imperial imposition.
In the absence of a male heir, Charles VI attempts to ensure the indivisibility of the Habsburg domains and the succession of his future daughter Maria Teresa.

eventos.titulo: Charles VII breaks up the continuity Habsburg
eventos.descripcion: In the course of the Austrian War of Succession, the elector Wittelsbach Carlos Alberto obtained the imperial crown and showed that dignity remained elective, even after centuries of Habsburg dominance.

eventos.titulo: Francis I Opens Habsburga's House - Lorena
eventos.descripcion: The election of Francisco Esteban returns the crown to the dynastic environment of Mary Teresa and creates the Habsburgo-Lorraine line.
Joseph II succeeded his father as emperor and, after 1780, tried to reform the Habsburg domains quickly, repeatedly colliding with territorial and corporate privileges.
The revolution in France alters the European political balance and makes the fate of Mary Antonieta, sister of Joseph II and Leopold II, an international dynastic problem.
Francis II inherits the imperial crown in the midst of revolutionary war. As 1800 arrived, the old Empire still existed, but it was facing a transformation that would end a few years later.

eventos.titulo: The battle and help of Vienna
eventos.descripcion: The relief army led by John III Sobieski, with Polish, Habsburg and Holy Roman Empire forces, breaks the Ottoman siege of Vienna on 12 September 1683. The victory opens a new phase of the war in Hungary and strengthens the rise of the Habsburg monarchy in central Europe.

eventos.titulo: The Hungarian Rebellion Openes a Door to the Sultan
eventos.descripcion: Imre Thököly leads Hungarian opposition to the Habsburgs and seeks Ottoman support. The internal conflict within Leopold I’s monarchy becomes entangled with imperial rivalry in central Europe.

eventos.titulo: Leopold and Sobieski pacts mutual relief
eventos.descripcion: With papal mediation, Leopold I and John III Sobieski agree on a defensive alliance. If Vienna or Krakow are attacked, the other sovereign must come to the aid of the ally.

The great visir Kara Mustafa leads the Ottoman army to Vienna. Leopold leaves the capital and Ernst Rüdiger von Starhemberg organizes the defense while fortifications suffer weeks of siege and mine work.

eventos.titulo: Polish, Imperial and German Princes Reunited
eventos.descripcion: Charles V of Lorraine coordinates the imperial forces and joins forces from Bavaria, Saxony and other territories of the Empire. Sobieski arrives with the Polish army and takes over the command of the relief operation.

eventos.titulo: From saving Vienna to passing to an offensive
eventos.descripcion: After the victory a new Holy League is formed. The Habsburgans, Poland and Venice transform an emergency defense into a prolonged war against the Ottoman Empire.
The conquest of Buda shows that Vienna was not an isolated episode. The war begun in 1683 develops into Habsburg expansion across Hungary and permanently alters the balance of central Europe.
Ivan Asen II defeats the Ripple and takes the second Bulgarian Empire to one of its most influential moments.
Serbian King Stefan Dušan holds his Imperial title at Skopje, an expression of Serbian's extraordinary territorial growth in the XIV century.
The battle of Kosovo caused the death of Prince Lazar and became a decisive milestone of Ottoman penetration and Serbian historic memory.
The campaign of 1462 pitted Vlad III against Mehmed II and opened a new struggle for the Wallachian throne, in which Radu the Fair received Ottoman support.
The forces of Mehmed II conquer the kingdom of Bosnia; the last king, Stephen Tomašević, is captured and executed.
Juana had chosen Louis of Anjou as heir, but Carlos of Durazzo conquered the kingdom. His death and that of Juana left the next generation a war between Anjou and Durazzo, not a peaceful succession.

people.resumen: He associated his daughter Tamar with the throne to secure the succession of the Bagrationi. His policy of expansion and his conflicts with the aristocracy set the stage for the Georgian monarchy at the end of the 12th century.

She ruled in her own right and brought Georgia to a period of great influence in the Caucasus. Military expansion, cultural patronage and support for the emergence of Trebizond connected her reign to the Byzantine world. Her children George IV and Rusudan succeeded her.

Second husband of Tamar and prominent military leader of his kingdom. His position as a consort and his victories supported the authority of the queen, without making it the origin of the Bagrationi's inheritance rights.

He inherited the Tamar monarchy, but the first clashes with the Mongols changed the prospects of the kingdom's expansion. His death left a younger son, David, and the crown passed to his sister Rusuman.

The Khwarazmian invasion and subsequent Mongol pressure broke the position achieved by her mother Tamar. Rusudan’s reign marks Georgia’s transition from expansion to tribute and outside intervention in the succession.

Son of Rusudan, he shared the crown with his cousin David VII by Mongol decision. After rebelling, he consolidated his power in the west, where the division of Georgia gave rise to the Imeretian monarchy under the same dynasty.

Son of George IV and cousin of David Narin, he received Mongol confirmation to share the throne. His government was tied to the Ilkhanate’s campaigns and fiscal demands; after the western separation he retained the eastern core.

He reigned in eastern Georgia under the Iljanate and participated in his campaigns. His execution by order of the Khan illustrates how far the sovereignty of the Bagrationi depended on the policy of the Mongolian court.

Lord of Samtsje, he ruled a border between Georgia, the Mongolian world and Trebizond. The marriages of his daughters link his house with the Bagrationi and the Grand Komnenoi; his grandson George V grew up in his surroundings.

Beka I's daughter and her wife Demetrio II. Through her, George V. was linked to the house of Samtzje, whose support was important during her childhood and in the reconstruction of her regal authority.

He strengthened royal authority and reunited fragmented territories under Mongol domination. The recovery was gradual: numismatic evidence qualifies any image of a complete and immediate break with the Ilkhanate. He maintained relations with Italian merchants and the powers of the eastern Mediterranean.
The daughter of Beka I of Samtsje and wife of Reebeng II. The opposition of Andronicus II to this marriage reveals that the family alliances of the Black Sea could contradict Constantinople's plans.

It promoted Georgian legal codification, printing and written culture. His career was conditioned by Persian investiture, Ottoman pressure and Russian aid that failed to consolidate his power; he ended up exiled in Russia.
A daughter of Vakhtang VI and wife of Teimuraz II, she linked the branches of Kartli and Kakheti. She was the mother of Heraclius II, who united both crowns in 1762.

His collaboration with Nader Shah favored the recognition of his power in Kartli. He and his son Heraclio ruled neighbouring crowns and sought external support to support their position after the collapse of the Nader empire.

He gathered Kartli and Kakheti in 1762 and tried to strengthen the eastern kingdom. The Gueorguievsk treaty linked him to Russia, but did not prevent Aga Mohamed Khan's attack on Tbilis in 1795. His career connects Georgian politics with Persia and Russian expansion.

He inherited the reunification promoted by George V. His reign coincided with the Black Death and a change in regional balance after the weakening of the Iljanate. His son Bagrat V continued the royal line.

The invasion of Tamerlán culminated in the seizure of Tbilis and his captivity in 1386. He was released, but the Western campaigns and rebellions eroded the authority he had inherited. His sons George VII and Constantine I were kings.

He resisted the repeated expeditions of Tamerlan and ended up negotiating a submission that allowed the Christian monarchy to be preserved. The military devastation weakened the resources of the crown and promoted the autonomy of the regional authorities.

He succeeded his brother George VII. His alliance with Shirvan brought him into conflict with the Qara Qoyunlu; he was captured and executed. Several branches that later contested the Georgian monarchy descended from his children.

He tried to rebuild the kingdom after the Tamerlán campaigns and to recover rents and fortresses for the crown. He associated his children with power, a successor solution that also facilitated the subsequent division. He abdicated to enter a monastery.

His brief reign continued the restoration begun by Alexander I while his brothers exercised regional power. He died without an heir to consolidate his line; the succession opened the way to George VIII and renewed disputes among the Bagrationi.

The son of Alexander I and brother of Vajtang IV, he participated in the distribution of power among the royal princes. His son Constantine II would retain Kartli when the monarchy was fragmented. Their numbering and the scope of their authority vary between sources.

The Western rebellion and its capture by the atabeg of Samtskhe broke its authority. After losing control of Kartli, he established his own monarchy in Kakheti. It is the same person known there as George I, origin of the later Kakheti royal branch.

Son of Constantine I and father of Bagrat VI. His position in genealogy allows us to understand that the branch that ended up ruling Imereti came from the Georgian royal family itself, even though it faced other descendants of that house.

He was declared king in the west and then extended his authority to Kartli. His ascension accelerated the fragmentation of the kingdom: George VIII retained Kakheti and other princes retained their own bases. His son Alexander continued the royal branch of Imereti.

He disputed the legacy of the united monarchy, but eventually recognized the separation of Kakheti and Imereti. His kingdom was centered in Kartli. His children continued to the royal line and the main branch of Mukhrani.

The rivalry with Kakheti and the safapivid expansion conditioned his reign. He temporarily incorporated the neighbouring kingdom, which later regained its autonomy. His abdication left the crown first to his brother and then to his son Luarsab.

Brother of David X, he assumed the crown after his abdication and gave it to his nephew Luarsab. His brief government links two generations of the Bagrationi in a period of increasing Persian intervention.

He defended Kartli's autonomy from his Safer campaigns. He died as a result of his battle with Garisi and his son Simon continued his resistance. The sources differ about some years of his reign, here from 1527 to 1556.

people.nombre: Tamar of Imereti, Queen of Kartli
people.resumen: The daughter of Agrat III of Imereti, her marriage with Luarsab I united the two western and eastern branches of the Bagratii. She was the mother of Simon I and David XI, and her challenges followed different policies with respect to saving power.

He first fought the safavid intervention and spent years in captivity in Persia. Freed to fight the Ottomans, he re-ruled before falling prisoner to them. His two stages of government were separated so as not to present captivity as effective power.

Known as Daud Khan after converting to Islam, he was promoted by the Safavids against his brother Simon. His control depended on Persian support and ended with the Ottoman offensive. His son Rostom would govern Kartli decades later.

The daughter of Levan of Kakheti and wife of Simon I of Kartli. Her family linked the two Eastern monarchies through their children and grandchildren; these marriages coexisted with political rivalries and with the intervention of Persia and the Ottomans.

He took over the government after his father Simon was captured by the Ottomans. He cooperated with Abbas I against them and tried to open contacts with Russia. His offspring connects the succession of Kartli with the court of Teimuraz I of Kakheti.

His reign ended under the pressure of Abbas I, who lured him to Persia and held him captive. He was executed after refusing to convert to Islam. The Georgian Church venerated him as a martyr, linking his memory to the religious defense of the kingdom.

Raised in the Persian court environment, he was installed by Abbas I after the fall of Luarsab II. His authority depended on the safavid presence and was limited outside the centers that he controlled.

Son of Bagrat VII, he inherited a power closely dependent on Persia. The Georgian rebellion of 1625 dislocated its authority and favored Teimuraz I. His death closed another safe attempt to stabilize Kartli through this dynastic branch.

His career in the Safavid administration preceded a long reign in Kartli. He combined loyalty to the shah with agreements with local nobles and protection of Christian institutions. After defeating Teimuraz, he extended his authority into Kakheti and arranged a succession by adoption.
Son of Constantine II, he founded the princely branch of Mukhrani. His descendants reached the crown of Kartli with Vajtang V, so this line does not appear as a family isolated from the royal trunk.
He continued the Mukhrani branch founded by his father Bagrat. His descendants link the first princes of this domain to the seventeenth-century kings of Kartli.

Prince of Mukhrani and father of Vajtang V. He participated in the Georgian resistance to the Safavids and died in Marabda. His son then reached the crown by means of a policy of understanding with Persia.

From Mukhrani, he was adopted as heir by Rostom and recognized by the shah. He extended the influence of his family towards Kakheti and Imereti through his children. His career combines Bagrationi legitimacy with the Safavid investiture.

He alternated the throne of Kartli with the military service to the shah. After losing the crown and recovering it nominally, he led safe forces in Afghanistan, where he died in a rebellion. The periods away from the kingdom are distinguished from their present government.

Son of Vajtang V and father of Vajtang VI. He was responsible for the Georgian government and the Safavid court. His children were candidates for the throne at a time when the Persian investiture and local control did not always match.

He received the crown while continuing to serve the safavids outside Georgia. He died during the Kandahar campaign. Vajtang, his brother, administered Kartli, so his title is not represented as a continuous effective government.

Brother of Vajtang VI, he obtained the throne first with Persian support and then under Ottoman domination. His changes in alliance and confession reflect the struggle for Kartli between the two powers and the factions of the royal family.

He consolidated the kingdom established by George VIII through flexible diplomacy with the neighbouring powers. He died in a coup led by his son George, an episode that opened another dispute within the royal branch itself.

He took power after his father's death and tried to expand to Kartli. His defeat and captivity allowed David X to temporarily incorporate Kakheti. His son Levan would then regain the independence of the kingdom.

He restored the Kakheti monarchy after the occupation of Kartli. His long reign sought stability through agreements with Persia and contacts with Russia. The marriages of his children linked Kakheti to the other houses in the Caucasus.

He sought Russian protection without completely breaking up with Persia. His son David briefly removed him from power; after he had recovered him, he died in another family coup led by Constantine. The two stages of his reign are separate.

He deposed his father Alexander II and occupied the throne for about a year. His death allowed Alexander to return. Through his wife Ketevan and son Teimuraz, his line became associated with resistance to Abbas I.

Raised in Persia, he had his father Alexander II killed, but his rule provoked a rebellion led by Ketevan and he died before consolidating his power. His case shows the limits of Safavid intervention in the succession.

Widow of David I, defended the rights of her son Teimuraz and intervened in the Kakhetin government. She was held hostage in Persia and was executed after refusing to convert to Islam. Her religious memory transcended Georgia through missionary testimonies.

Poet and king, he alternated resistance, negotiation and exile in the face of the pressure of Abbas I and his successors. The 1625 rebellion allowed him to return and extend his authority to Kartli, but Rostom eventually moved him. His family suffered captivity, executions and displacements.

Daughter of George X of Kartli and wife of Teimuraz I of Kakheti. The marriage strengthened cooperation between the two branches during their wars against Persia. Her children linked this generation to the later kings of Kakheti and Imereti.

Son of Teimuraz I and Jorashan, fought in the fight against Rostom and died in the battle of Magharo. His son Heraclio continued the Kakheti royal line, from which Teimuraz II and Heraclio II would come.

He spent part of his youth in Russia and ultimately accepted Safavid investiture. He ruled Kartli and later received the crown of Kakheti, which his son David administered locally. His career connects the Bagrationi exiles with service to the shah.

He administered Kakheti while his father remained in Persia and then received confirmation of the crown. The incursions from Dagestan and the demands of the Shah limited their government. His brothers Constantine and Teimuraz succeeded him.

He received the Kakhetian crown in the context of the Safavid collapse and briefly occupied Tiflis in front of Vakhtang VI. The Ottoman intervention altered his alliances and ended his death. His brother Teimuraz then reorganized the eastern power.
A son of Bagrat VI, he defended the western throne against Constantine II. His consolidation in Imereti helped make the division of Georgia permanent. The crown passed to his son Bagrat III.

He tried to subdue the great western princes and extend his influence over Samtskhe. Ottoman intervention and rivalries with Mingrelia and Guria limited that policy. His daughter Tamar linked his house to the kings of Kartli.

He ruled between conflicts with the princes of Mingrelia and Guria and with growing Ottoman pressure. His sons and nephews would compete for a crown whose power depended increasingly on aristocratic alliances.

He came to the throne as a teenager and had to face family rebellions and intervention from the neighboring principalities. He was deposed and died captive, leaving open the struggle for control of the Western monarchy.

The son of Bagrat III, belonged to the generation that disputed Western power to his relatives. His sons Rostom and George III successively occupied the throne, maintaining the genealogical continuity of the royal house.
He depended on Mingrelia's backing to attain and regain the throne. His reign included a break during the intervention of Simon of Kartli and his Western rivals, so two mandates are recorded.

His monarchy lived side by side with the growing strength of Levan II Dadiani of Mingrelia. The clashes between the two limited the crown’s ability to control the Georgian West. His son Alexander III continued that dispute.

He sought to strengthen the crown in front of the Dadiani and took advantage of Mingrelia's succession changes to expand its influence. His marriage to Darejan, daughter of Teimuraz I, linked Imereti to the Kakheti branch.

Daughter of Teimuraz I, was Queen Consort of Imereti and a decisive figure in her subsequent disputes. After Alexander III's death she intervened against Bagrat V and promoted Vajtang Tchutchunashvili. She died during another Western court crisis.

It was deposed, blinded and restored repeatedly. His Governments showed a monarchy conditioned by nobility factions, marriages and the intervention of the neighbouring principals. Each restoration appears separate to preserve the chronology of disputes.

Son of Vajtang V, was installed at different times in Kakheti and Imereti. His repeated losses of the throne led him to Russian exile, where he developed his literary activity. Unite the three territorial branches without making them a single permanent crown.

Son of Bagrat V, returned to the throne with Ottoman support and faced the factions that favoured Archil. His two reigns ended in new expulsions; his death did not end the rivalry between the two lines.

Son of Alexander IV, briefly occupied a crown disputed by great lords and candidates Bagrationi. His murder opened another phase of intervention by the Gurieli and Abashidze in the government of Imereti.

He regained the throne several times through changing alliances and Ottoman support. The interventions of the Gurieli and other nobles interrupted their authority. His sons Alexander V and George IX extended the royal branch during the 18th century.

Its long political period included depositions and restorations, under Ottoman influence and with strong aristocratic intervention. He was the father of Solomon I and of Prince Archil, connecting the last two generations of unrighteous kings.

Alexander V's brother was promoted during one of his expulsions. His brief government illustrates how factions could replace the king without leaving the same Bagrationi family. His son David II would fight the crown again.

A brother of Alexander V, he occupied the throne during another interruption of Alexander’s rule. Rivalry among the princes of this generation later continued in the struggle between his son Teimuraz and Solomon I.

He tried to limit the power of the great lords and combat the slave trade. Khresili’s victory reinforced his position against the Ottomans, although he suffered a temporary deposition. His policy sought greater autonomy for the Western monarchy.

Son of Mamuka, was installed with Ottoman support in front of his cousin Solomon I. His defeat allowed the restoration of this. The episode shows that the divisions of the royal house facilitated the outside intervention.

It was made with the crown after the death of Solomon I and it was disputed with the future Solomon II. He was briefly defeated and restored and ended up in exile. Its two stages remain separate from those of its rival.
Brother of Solomon I and father of Solomon II. His marriage to Helena, daughter of Heracli II, linked the last royal generation of Imereti with the united monarchy of Kartli-Kajetia.
Daughter of Heraclius II and wife of Prince Archil of Imereti. She was the mother of Solomon II: this connection helps explain the eastern support for her candidacy to the Western throne.

He joined power with the support of his grandfather Heraclio II and fought the crown for David II. The Russian expansion ended with its deposition in 1810. He died in exile in Trebizond, after trying to recover the kingdom.

The last king of Kartli-Kakheti inherited a monarchy weakened by the Persian invasion and family disputes. He applied for Russian protection, but his death preceded the annexation of the kingdom. The dynastic succession did not become another effective reign.

Georgian princess, took the name Eudoxia and married Manuel III. She was the mother of Alejo IV. Her file connects two Black Sea courts without attributing a territorial government to her for her status as consort.

translatedSource.resumen: Hainaut was a county distinct from Flanders, although the two inheritances shared several medieval holders. The rivalry between Avesnes and Dampierre ultimately placed it in the Avesnes descendants of Margaret II. Through the rights of his mother, Adelaide of Holland, John II united Hainaut with Holland and Zeeland in 1299. The same counts could have different regnal numbers in each territory. The succession passed to Margaret of Bavaria and then her Wittelsbach descendants, until Jacqueline’s disputes and the cession to Philip the Good. The county retained its identity within the Burgundian lands.

eventos.titulo: The murder of Juan Sin Mido
eventos.descripcion: John the Fearless is assassinated at Montereau. Philip the Good inherits Burgundy and draws closer to the English side.
Joan is captured by Burgundian forces near Compiègne and falls into English hands; she will be executed at Rouen in 1431.

eventos.titulo: Foundation of the Order of the Golden Toison
eventos.descripcion: Philip the Good founded the Order of the Golden Toison in the context of his marriage to Isabel of Portugal.
Philip the Good is reunited with Charles VII and breaks his alliance with England.
Charles the Bold succeeds Philip the Good and attempts to consolidate a Burgundian territorial bloc between France and the Empire.

eventos.titulo: Battle of Nancy and death of Charles the Bold
eventos.descripcion: Charles dies without a male heir. His daughter Mary receives an inheritance immediately contested by Louis XI of France.
Marriage links the Borgognon heritage to the Habsburg and changes the political balance of Western Europe.
The agreement returns Artois and the County of Burgundy to the heritage of Maria de Burgundy, while the Duchy of Burgundy remains in French hands.
Charles V demands Luther to retract. The reformer's refusal and the political protection of Frederick the Wise transform a theological dispute into a constitutional problem of the Empire.
The imperial forces defeat the French army and capture King Francis I.
Mooted imperial troops loot Rome during the Italian Wars.
The agreement legally accepts the coexistence of Catholic and Lutheran territories within the Empire and recognizes that religious unity can no longer be restored by mere imperial imposition.
Charles V gradually distributes his domains between the Spanish branch and the Austrian branch of the Habsburgés.
Philip II's naval expedition against England fails after fighting, logistical problems and adverse time.

eventos.titulo: Charles V is elected King of Romans
eventos.descripcion: The succession of Maximilian I makes the imperial choice a European competition. Carlos brings together the imperial crown with a dynastic heritage that extends from the Netherlands to Spain and America.
In the absence of a male heir, Charles VI attempts to ensure the indivisibility of the Habsburg domains and the succession of his future daughter Maria Teresa.

eventos.titulo: Charles VII breaks up the continuity Habsburg
eventos.descripcion: In the course of the Austrian War of Succession, the elector Wittelsbach Carlos Alberto obtained the imperial crown and showed that dignity remained elective, even after centuries of Habsburg dominance.

eventos.titulo: Francis I Opens Habsburga's House - Lorena
eventos.descripcion: The election of Francisco Esteban returns the crown to the dynastic environment of Mary Teresa and creates the Habsburgo-Lorraine line.
Joseph II succeeded his father as emperor and, after 1780, tried to reform the Habsburg domains quickly, repeatedly colliding with territorial and corporate privileges.
The revolution in France alters the European political balance and makes the fate of Mary Antonieta, sister of Joseph II and Leopold II, an international dynastic problem.
Francis II inherits the imperial crown in the midst of revolutionary war. As 1800 arrived, the old Empire still existed, but it was facing a transformation that would end a few years later.
Philip Melanchthon presents to Charles V a systematic exhibition of the Lutheran faith, backed by several princes and cities of the Empire.
Charles V defeats the League of Esmalcalda and captures its two great leaders, but military victory does not succeed in restoring the religious unity of the Empire.
The death of Francis of Anjou makes Henry of Navarra an alleged heir. Enrique de Guisa reorganizes the Catholic League, backed from Spain, to prevent a Protestant from inheriting the French crown.

eventos.titulo: Pius V gets the Holy League
eventos.descripcion: Pius V has an agreement between the Hispanic Monarchy, Venice and the Pontifical States. Philip II provides an essential part of the resources and his stepbrother Don Juan of Austria receives the supreme command of the Allied fleet.
